# The index of the order generated by a block power

<a id="statement"></a>
## An integral index independent of the delay

Let \(A,B\in\mathbb Z[T]\) be nonzero polynomials with no common complex root, \(A\) monic and \(B(0)=\pm1\).
Take coprime positive integers \(n,g\) with \(n+g\deg A>g\deg B\), and put
\[
 P(X)=X^n A(X^g)-B(X^g),\quad
 O=\mathbb Z[X]/(P),\quad x=X\bmod P,\quad t=x^g,\quad O_0=\mathbb Z[t]\subset O.
\]
Both rings are free of rank \(\deg P\) over \(\mathbb Z\), and
\[
                         [O:O_0]=|\operatorname{Res}(A,B)|^{g(g-1)/2}. \tag{1}
\]
As a module over \(R=\mathbb Z[T,T^{-1}]\), with \(T\) acting by \(t\), \(O/O_0\) depends only on \(g,A,B\).
For \(g>1\) it has generators \(e_1,\ldots,e_{g-1}\) and relations
\[
    A e_1=0,\qquad A e_{i+1}=B e_i\quad(1\le i<g-1),
                    \qquad B e_{g-1}=0.                               \tag{2}
\]
For \(g=1\) the quotient is zero.
The ideal \((A,B)^{g-1}\) annihilates the module.
The hypotheses allow repeated roots of \(P\) and any constant coefficient of \(A\).

For each monic irreducible factor \(S\mid P\) and any root \(\alpha\) of \(S\), the fields \(\mathbb Q(\alpha^g)\) and \(\mathbb Q(\alpha)\) are equal.
The abelian group \(\mathbb Z[\alpha]/\mathbb Z[\alpha^g]\) is a quotient of (2).
The product of all the individual order indices, counted with the multiplicities of their factors in \(P\), divides (1).
Thus every one of these orders agrees with its power suborder after localization at any prime not dividing \(\operatorname{Res}(A,B)\).

For \(A(T)=(T-2)(T-3)\), \(B(T)=\pm(1-2T)(1-3T)\), the entire additive group is
\[
       O/O_0\ \cong\ \bigoplus_{j=1}^{g-1}
                 \left(\mathbb Z/15^j\mathbb Z\ \oplus\
                       \mathbb Z/40^j\mathbb Z\right).                 \tag{3}
\]
In particular its order is \(600^{g(g-1)/2}\) and its exponent is \(120^{g-1}\).
This gives the integral indices associated with the [equalities of power fields for prime blocks](Yin_C_G0345_v203.md#heights), without a lower bound on \(n\) beyond the degree condition above.

<a id="presentation"></a>
## Eliminating the delay from the module

The polynomial \(P\) is monic with constant coefficient \(\pm1\), so \(O\) has the usual power basis and \(x\) is a unit.
Multiplication by \(t=x^g\) on \(O\) is an integral automorphism; its characteristic polynomial has constant coefficient \(\pm1\).
Cayley–Hamilton therefore gives \(t^{-1}\in\mathbb Z[t]\) and shows that \(1,t,\ldots,t^{\deg P-1}\) span \(O_0\).

The map \(T\mapsto X^g,\ Y\mapsto X^n\) gives an isomorphism
\[
             R[Y]/(Y^g-T^n)\ \simeq\ \mathbb Z[X,X^{-1}].
\]
Indeed \(1,Y,\ldots,Y^{g-1}\) is an \(R\)-basis, and the exponents \(0,n,\ldots,(g-1)n\) represent all classes modulo \(g\) exactly once.
To pass to \(O\), impose the further equation \(A(T)Y-B(T)=0\).
Its ideal as an \(R\)-module is generated by its products with \(1,Y,\ldots,Y^{g-1}\).
The summand generated by \(1\) maps onto \(O_0\).
After quotienting by that summand, the images \(e_i\) of \(Y^i\), \(1\le i<g\), obey exactly (2); the term \(T^nA(T)\) in the last product has disappeared.
For \(r=g-1\), the relations give \(A^i e_i=0\) and \(B^{r-i+1}e_i=0\).
Every product \(A^a B^b\) with \(a+b=r\) therefore kills each generator.

<a id="index"></a>
## Computing the determinant with repeated roots allowed

For any monic polynomial \(Q\) of degree \(d\), let \(I_g(Q)\) denote the determinant of the columns \(1,X^g,\ldots,X^{(d-1)g}\) reduced modulo \(Q\) in its power basis.
If \(z_1,\dots,z_d\) are all the roots with multiplicity, then
\[
 I_g(Q)=\prod_{i<j}D_g(z_i,z_j),\qquad
                 D_g(u,v)=\sum_{b=0}^{g-1}u^{g-1-b}v^b .
\]
For distinct roots this follows by evaluation of both bases and the Vandermonde determinant.
The identity for repeated roots follows by continuity in the root tuple: monic division gives polynomial entries in the coefficients of \(Q\), and the right side is polynomial in the roots.

Take \(Q=P\), \(d=\deg P\), and write \(\mu_g\) for the \(g\)-th roots of unity.
Since \(D_g\) is symmetric and \(D_g(u,u)=g u^{g-1}\), multiplying over all ordered pairs gives
\[
 \left|\prod_{i,j}D_g(z_i,z_j)\right|
       =g^d |I_g(P)|^2
       =\prod_j\prod_{\zeta\in\mu_g\setminus\{1\}} |P(\zeta z_j)|.
\]
Here \(|\prod_j z_j|=1\) by the constant coefficient, and the last equality uses \(D_g(u,v)=\prod_{\zeta\ne1}(u-\zeta v)\).
At a root of \(P\) we have \(P(\zeta z_j)=(\zeta^n-1)z_j^n A(z_j^g)\).
Raising to the \(n\)-th power permutes \(\mu_g\), so \(\prod_{\zeta\ne1}|\zeta^n-1|=g\).
Canceling \(g^d\) and using the unit constant again gives
\[
                  |I_g(P)|^2
                     =\left|\prod_j A(z_j^g)\right|^{g-1}.
\]
The product inside the absolute value is \(\operatorname{Res}(P,A(X^g))\).
Interchanging the two polynomials and evaluating at the roots of \(A(X^g)\) gives absolute value \(|\operatorname{Res}(A,B)|^g\), since at each such root \(z\) we have \(P(z)=-B(z^g)\), and every root of \(A\) occurs with \(g\) preimages counted with multiplicity.
This argument includes a zero root of \(A\), and for \(A=1\) uses the empty product.
The resultant is nonzero, so the spanning columns for \(O_0\) are independent of full rank, and their absolute determinant proves (1).

<a id="factors"></a>
## Quotients at individual irreducible factors

Projection to \(\mathbb Z[\alpha]\) sends \(O_0\) onto \(\mathbb Z[\alpha^g]\), so induces a surjection of the additive quotients.
Their finiteness gives the equality of rational fields and the individual prime-to-resultant assertion.
Alternatively \(\alpha^n=B(\alpha^g)/A(\alpha^g)\), where the denominator is nonzero by coprimality at the roots, and Bézout for \(n,g\) recovers \(\alpha\) from \(\alpha^n,\alpha^g\).

Factor \(P\) into monic irreducibles, treating each occurrence as a separate entry in the list.
In the pair product for \(I_g(P)\), pairs from one entry give \(I_g(S)\), whose absolute value is exactly its individual index by the power-basis computation above.
For two different entries, the product of \(D_g(z_i,z_j)\) over all pairs between them is an integer.
It is an algebraic integer invariant under Galois conjugation because each list of roots is separately invariant, including when the entries are two copies of the same factor.
All the pair products are nonzero since \(I_g(P)\ne0\).
Taking absolute values proves the asserted divisibility of the product of the individual indices.

<a id="two-three"></a>
## The two additive summands at each exponent

Take the blocks in (3) and suppose \(r=g-1>0\).
Form the presentation (2) first over \(\mathbb Z[T]\); inverting \(T\) then gives the required \(R\)-module.
The same relations imply that \(A^r\) annihilates the polynomial-ring module.
The ideals generated by \((T-2)^r\) and \((T-3)^r\) are comaximal since \(2-3\) is a unit.
The Chinese remainder theorem therefore splits the module into its two components over \(\mathbb Z[q]/(q^r)\), with \(q=T-a\), \(a=2,3\) respectively.

To simplify (2) over either component, view its relation matrix as the transpose of multiplication by \(A U-B V\) from homogeneous polynomials of degree \(r-1\) in \(U,V\) to those of degree \(r\).
Indeed, in the respective monomial bases the transposed columns give \(A e_1,\ A e_{i+1}-B e_i,\ -B e_r\).
An invertible linear change in \(U,V\) induces invertible basis changes in both degrees, hence leaves the transposed cokernel isomorphic.
In the component at \(a\), write \(A=qC\) with \(C=T-a'\), where \(a'\) is the other root.
The constant term of \(C\) in \(q\) is \(a-a'=\pm1\), so \(C\) is invertible modulo \(q^r\).
Writing \(B=u+qV_0\) with \(u=B(a)\) gives
\[
                  AU-BV=q(CU-V_0V)-uV .
\]
The change \(U'=CU-V_0V,\ V'=V\) is invertible, so the module has the presentation (2) with \(A,B\) replaced by \(q,u\).

In this presentation \(q e_1=0,\ q e_i=u e_{i-1}\) for \(2\le i\le r\), and \(u e_r=0\).
It follows that \(u^{r-i+1}e_i=0\) for every \(i\), and the \(e_i\) already generate the underlying abelian group.
Conversely, on the direct sum of cyclic groups with the \(i\)-th generator of order \(|u|^{r-i+1}\), define \(q\) by this same shift.
It is well-defined because the order of \(u e_{i-1}\) divides \(|u|^{r-i+1}\), it satisfies \(q^r=0\), and all the indicated module relations hold.
The maps in the two directions taking each generator to its namesake are inverse, so these are the exact cyclic orders.
Here \(|B(2)|=15\), \(|B(3)|=40\), and \(\gcd(a,B(a))=1\) in both components.
Consequently multiplication by \(a\) is invertible on each component, and so is \(T=a+q\) because \(q\) is nilpotent.
Inverting \(T\) preserves both groups, proving (3) and its exponent formula.
These conclusions concern the entire quotient and its images; (3) does not assign its summands to particular rational factors of \(P\).
